core: Globalization as a HISTORICAL development: the accelerating integration of the world's economies, cultures, and politics in the late 20th and early 21st centuries
Postwar foundations: the United Nations (1945), the Bretton Woods institutions (IMF and World Bank, 1944), and the trade regime GATT (1947) becoming the WTO (1995)
Drivers that lowered the cost of distance: container shipping (SS Ideal X, 1956), jet travel, telecommunications and the internet, and the post-Cold-War opening of markets
Effects: vastly expanded trade and global supply chains, cultural exchange, and a large reduction in global extreme poverty
Criticisms: rising inequality within some countries, job dislocation, environmental strain, cultural homogenization, and loss of sovereignty
That globalization is not new but has deep roots (Silk Roads, Columbian Exchange) now vastly accelerated
That the 'good vs bad' verdict is a genuine, unresolved debate
supporting: Multinational corporations and their role in politics, labor, and the environment
Named examples: NAFTA (1994), the euro (1999), Rana Plaza collapse (2013), Brexit
outOfScope: Economic THEORY of trade (comparative advantage, exchange rates) — the economics subject
Human-geography treatment of globalization and development — the human-geography subject
The end of the Cold War, decolonization, imperialism, and the Industrial Revolution as their own topics (named here, not owned)

claims.claim: The Bretton Woods institutions — the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank — were created in 1944 to stabilize the postwar international economy; the World Bank initially financed reconstruction and later shifted toward development lending.
The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) was signed in 1947 to reduce trade barriers; it was replaced in 1995 by the World Trade Organization (WTO), which China joined in 2001.
The United Nations was founded in 1945: its Charter was signed in San Francisco on 26 June 1945 by 50 of the 51 original member states and entered into force on 24 October 1945.

Modern container shipping began with the voyage of the SS Ideal X, a converted tanker that carried 58 containers from Port Newark, New Jersey, on 26 April 1956 under trucking entrepreneur Malcom McLean; containerization sharply reduced the cost and time of loading cargo and helped make global supply chains possible.

According to World Bank estimates (Poverty and Inequality Platform, 2025 update), the number of people in extreme poverty fell from about 2.31 billion in 1990 to about 808 million in 2025 — roughly 44% to about 10% of the world's population — measured at the international poverty line of $3.00 a day in 2021 prices; much of the reduction was concentrated in Asia, especially China.

Modern globalization drew sustained criticism: multinational supply chains have been linked to sweatshop labor (the 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse in Bangladesh killed 1,134 workers), to environmental harm such as deforestation and water depletion, to concerns about cultural homogenization, and to concerns about lost national sovereignty (a theme of the United Kingdom's exit from the European Union).

Globalization is not new: long-distance exchange networks such as the Silk Roads and the post-1492 Columbian Exchange (the transfer of crops, animals, people, and diseases between the Americas and the Old World) linked distant regions centuries earlier; what is distinctive about the modern era is the vastly greater speed, volume, and reach of integration.

Whether globalization has been, on balance, beneficial or harmful is a genuine and unresolved debate: the same period saw both a historically large reduction in extreme poverty and real dislocation, inequality, and environmental strain, and historians and economists do not agree on a single verdict.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether globalization is 'good' or 'bad' on balance
positions: Advocates emphasize expanded trade, cheaper goods, cultural exchange, and the largest reduction in extreme poverty in recorded history, much of it in Asia.

Critics emphasize job dislocation in some advanced-economy industries, rising within-country inequality in some places, dangerous labor conditions in global supply chains, environmental strain, cultural homogenization, and erosion of national sovereignty.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented even-handedly as an unresolved debate; the lesson names both sides and does not declare a winner.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much of the poverty decline is attributable to globalization versus other factors (e.g., domestic policy in China and India)
positions: Global integration expanded export markets and investment that supported growth.
Much of the decline was concentrated in a few large Asian economies whose domestic reforms also drove growth, so globalization is not the sole cause.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the poverty figures to the World Bank and notes the concentration in Asia rather than claiming globalization as the sole cause.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft was generic boilerplate ('Globalization is a foundational concept in History...') with no specific dates, institutions, drivers, figures, or debate; all of it was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced empty boilerplate with dated, attributed history.

Did NOT reproduce the OpenStax text's 'nearly eighteen million manufacturing jobs' figure for 1993-2021: manufacturing-job change is driven by automation as well as trade and the exact count is contested, so the lesson describes job dislocation qualitatively and flags multiple causation instead of asserting a precise number.

Attributed the extreme-poverty figures to the World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform and dated them, and stated the specific international poverty line ($3.00/day, 2021 prices) because different lines yield different shares.
